outline.guidance: Open with a relatable pain point: dull, rough, or uneven skin texture that lotion alone never seems to fix. Explain that exfoliation is the missing step most people skip — and that the right natural body scrub can transform the effectiveness of everything applied afterward, including body lotion and body butter. Establish the post's promise: by the end, the reader will know exactly which scrub ingredients work best for their skin type, how to use a body scrub correctly, and how to build a routine that keeps skin soft and glowing. Keep the tone warm, knowledgeable, and conversational — not clinical. Naturally introduce the target keyword 'body scrub' and the phrase 'glowing skin' within the first two sentences.

outline.section: H2: What Is a Body Scrub and Why Does Your Skin Need It?
outline.guidance: Explain what a body scrub is: a topical exfoliant that uses physical particles (sugar, sea salt, ground botanicals) combined with a carrier oil or cream base to slough away dead skin cells from the surface of the body. Briefly describe the skin renewal cycle — the stratum corneum sheds dead cells roughly every 28 days, and buildup causes dullness, clogged pores, and reduced absorption of moisturizers. Cite a credible external source here (e.g., a PubMed article or American Academy of Dermatology resource on skin cell turnover) to support the science. Explain that regular exfoliation accelerates this process, reveals newer skin underneath, and significantly improves how well follow-up products like body lotion and body oil absorb. Avoid overly technical language. Use the phrase 'body scrub' at least twice and reference 'moisturizing body wash' and 'body oil for dry skin' naturally.

outline.section: H2: Physical vs. Chemical Exfoliation — Which Is Right for You?
outline.guidance: Briefly distinguish physical exfoliation (the kind body scrubs provide — manual friction with granular particles) from chemical exfoliation (AHAs, BHAs). For the purposes of this post, focus primarily on physical scrubs since that is the target keyword. Note that physical scrubs are preferred by many people for body use because the skin on the body is thicker and more tolerant than facial skin. Explain that the right physical exfoliant particle size matters: coarser particles like sea salt are better for normal to oily skin and rough areas like elbows and knees; finer particles like sugar are gentler and better for sensitive or dry skin. Mention that natural oil bases (coconut oil, jojoba oil) in a scrub double as moisturizers, making a good natural body scrub a two-in-one treatment. Include the keywords 'jojoba oil for skin' and 'body butter for dry skin' naturally in this context.

outline.section: H2: How to Choose the Best Natural Body Scrub for Your Skin Type
outline.guidance: This is the core educational section and a key differentiator. Break it into four clearly written sub-sections using H3s (see below). For each skin type, name the ideal exfoliant particle, the ideal carrier/oil base, and any ingredients to avoid. Use a consistent structure across all four skin types so readers can quickly find their type and get actionable guidance. This is where the post meaningfully beats all top-ranking competitor category pages which offer no skin-type guidance at all. Naturally reference 'best body lotion for dry skin,' 'body lotion for dry skin,' and 'best body oil' in the dry skin subsection. Keep the overall tone empowering — help the reader feel like they now have an expert in their corner.
keywords_to_include: best body lotion for dry skin

outline.section: H3: Body Scrub for Dry Skin
outline.guidance: Recommend finely-ground sugar as the ideal particle — it dissolves with water and is less abrasive than salt, reducing the risk of micro-tears in already-compromised skin. Recommend a rich oil base such as coconut oil or shea butter. Advise avoiding alcohol-based scrubs or very coarse salt scrubs which can strip moisture. Mention that dry skin benefits most from immediately following a scrub with a body lotion for dry skin or a body butter while skin is still slightly damp to lock in moisture. Include 'body butter for dry skin' and 'best body lotion for dry skin' naturally.
keywords_to_include: best body lotion for dry skin

outline.section: H3: Body Scrub for Sensitive Skin
outline.guidance: Recommend ultra-fine sugar or oat-based exfoliants. Emphasize fragrance-free or naturally-scented-only formulas to avoid irritation. Advise limiting exfoliation to once a week. Caution against scrubbing broken, irritated, or sunburned skin. Recommend patch-testing any new scrub. Note that a gentle, clean moisturizing body cream after exfoliation is essential for sensitive skin recovery.

outline.section: H3: Body Scrub for Oily or Acne-Prone Skin
outline.guidance: Recommend sea salt as a preferred exfoliant — it has natural purifying properties and a coarser texture that helps clear congested pores on the body. Note that back acne (bacne) and chest breakouts often improve with regular exfoliation that unclogs follicles. Recommend lightweight oil bases like jojoba oil, which is non-comedogenic. Suggest 2–3 times per week. Link naturally to body oil moisturizer as a follow-up. Include 'jojoba oil for skin' and 'body oil moisturizer.'

outline.section: H3: Body Scrub for Normal or Combination Skin
outline.guidance: Explain that normal and combination skin types have the most flexibility — both sugar and salt scrubs work well. Encourage experimenting with texture and scent preferences. Suggest 1–2 times per week as a good maintenance cadence. Recommend pairing with a natural body lotion or body oil after exfoliation for best results. Keep this brief and positive.

outline.section: H2: Key Ingredients to Look for in a Natural Body Scrub
outline.guidance: Walk through the most important clean, natural ingredients found in high-quality body scrubs and explain what each one does for the skin. Cover at minimum: (1) Sugar — gentle humectant exfoliant, dissolves safely; (2) Sea salt — mineral-rich, detoxifying, best for normal to oily skin; (3) Coconut oil — moisturizing carrier, contains lauric acid which has skin-supporting properties — include at least one external citation (e.g., a PubMed study on coconut oil and skin barrier function); (4) Jojoba oil — non-comedogenic, mimics skin's natural sebum, absorbs well; (5) Shea butter — deeply nourishing, ideal in scrubs targeting dry skin. Also briefly mention what to AVOID: synthetic fragrances, parabens, PEGs, microbeads (now banned in the US for environmental reasons). Framing the 'what to avoid' content positions Real Skin Care's natural formulations as the smart, clean choice without making any direct competitor comparisons.

outline.section: H2: How to Use a Body Scrub: Step-by-Step for Best Results
outline.guidance: Provide a practical, numbered how-to sequence that readers can follow immediately. Steps should include: (1) Start in the shower — wet skin thoroughly with warm (not hot) water to soften the skin surface; (2) Apply the scrub in circular motions, working from feet upward toward the heart to support circulation; (3) Focus on rough areas first — knees, elbows, heels; (4) Scrub gently — pressure should feel like a massage, never painful; (5) Rinse thoroughly; (6) Pat dry — do not rub; (7) Immediately apply a moisturizing body lotion, body cream, or body oil while skin is still slightly damp to seal in hydration. Emphasize step 7 strongly — this is where readers naturally connect to Real Skin Care's follow-up moisturizer products. Frequency guidance: 1–3 times per week depending on skin type (reference the skin-type section above). Keep tone practical and encouraging.

outline.section: H2: Completing Your Body Care Routine After Exfoliation
outline.guidance: This section bridges exfoliation to moisturization and is the key commercial bridge for Real Skin Care's product collections. Explain that a freshly exfoliated body is uniquely receptive to moisturizing ingredients — the removal of the dead skin barrier means active ingredients in lotions and creams penetrate more effectively. Make the case for choosing a natural, organic body lotion or body cream as the ideal follow-up. Describe the difference between body lotion (lighter, fast-absorbing, good for normal/oily skin), body cream (richer, longer-lasting, ideal for dry skin), and body butter (thickest, most intensive, great for very dry or eczema-prone skin) to help readers choose. Naturally weave in internal links here. Include keywords: 'body lotion for dry skin,' 'natural body lotion,' 'organic body lotion,' 'moisturizing body cream,' 'body butter for dry skin,' 'best body lotion for dry skin,' 'body oil for dry skin.'

outline.section: H2: Frequently Asked Questions About Body Scrubs
outline.guidance: Write 4 concise FAQ items that target real search behavior. Suggested questions: (1) How often should you use a body scrub? — Answer: 1–3 times per week depending on skin type; over-exfoliating can cause irritation. (2) Can you make a homemade body scrub for glowing skin? — Answer: Yes, a simple DIY body scrub can be made with sugar or sea salt and coconut or jojoba oil; briefly describe the concept but pivot to noting that a quality store-bought natural scrub ensures consistent ingredient ratios and stability. (3) Is a body scrub the same as a body wash? — Answer: No — a body wash cleanses; a body scrub exfoliates. Some moisturizing body washes contain mild exfoliants, but a dedicated scrub provides significantly more exfoliation. (4) What should I put on my skin after a body scrub? — Answer: Apply a natural body lotion, body cream, or body oil immediately after patting dry for best absorption. Format using natural question/answer prose, not bullet points, to maintain readability and FAQ schema eligibility.
